datasets.name: Gibson (Gibson tiny)
datasets.eval_protocol: Trained on the train split and evaluated on the validation split; the validation set was not used for hyperparameter tuning. Results use 5 test scenes and 200 episodes per scene (1,000 episodes total). Success requires stopping within 1 m of the goal; episodes are capped at 500 steps. Six goal categories are used.

datasets.name: Matterport3D (MP3D)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the standard train and test splits. Results use 10 test scenes and 200 episodes per scene (2,000 episodes total); one additional scene was excluded because it contained none of the six goal categories. Success requires stopping within 1 m of the goal; episodes are capped at 500 steps.

datasets.name: CVPR 2020 Habitat ObjectNav Challenge
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the Test-Challenge dataset with the challenge’s 21 goal categories. The paper reports SPL, success, and distance to goal; it does not state an episode count or further evaluation protocol.

baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same described heuristic local policy as Classical Mapping + FBE: a pretrained Mask R-CNN detects the goal object and an analytical planner moves toward it. Trained for 10 million frames.

controls.rules_out: A performance difference against this ablation supports a contribution from goal-oriented exploration beyond having a semantic map and a coverage-maximizing policy.

controls.rules_out: Comparing with conditions that add object and distance information isolates the contribution of those inputs from caption-only perception.

controls.name: Object information without relative distance
controls.detail: The '+ Obj' condition adds detected object information to the caption baseline but not the relative distance information; '+ Obj + Dis' adds distance as well.
controls.rules_out: Comparing these conditions assesses the incremental contribution of relative-distance information beyond object information.

datasets.name: Habitat 2020 ObjectNav Challenge (Matterport3D scenes)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 90 Matterport3D scenes with the standard train/val/test split and no scene overlap. The episode dataset specifies a start pose and target category. Valid viewpoints are navigable locations within 1 m of, or inside, the target’s oriented bounding box where the target is visible under oracle visibility; viewpoints are sampled on an R_agent/2 floor grid, and instances with no valid viewpoints are excluded. Episodes are filtered to have a shortest action path of at most 750 and a geodesic-to-Euclidean distance ratio of at least 1.05. Success is STOP within 0.1 m geodesic distance of a valid viewpoint. The paper’s table lists 2,803K Habitat episodes, but gives no challenge evaluation count by split.

datasets.name: RoboTHOR 2020 ObjectNav Challenge
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 75 simulated training scenes (60 for training and the remainder for validation), 4 real/simulated test-dev scenes, and 10 real test-challenge scenes; the challenge scenes have no overlap in wall layout or object instances with training/validation. Uses 12 target categories. In phase 2, tests on the 4 real scenes and their simulated counterparts; in phase 3, tests on the blind 10-scene real set. Evaluation considers RGB-only and RGB-plus-depth sensor settings. Success requires the target to be within 1 m and in the camera field of view; in real experiments, distance is measured using Super-NIA-3D localization modules and visibility is manually checked. The paper’s table lists 34K RoboTHOR episodes overall, but gives no evaluation episode count by phase.

metrics.name: Success
metrics.caveat: Binary success does not distinguish a gross failure from a near miss and gives no indication of partial progress; the paper recommends assessing efficiency alongside success, using SPL.

metrics.name: ObjectNav-SPL
metrics.caveat: Because it multiplies path efficiency by binary success, failures are all scored zero and the metric can have high variance, especially with noisy actuation. It does not penalize in-place turning, and it is unsuitable for comparisons across datasets or portions with substantially different optimal path lengths. The paper discusses action count or energy as possible alternatives and says a future metric should replace SPL, but does not evaluate one.

confounds.name: Collision sliding can let agents exploit non-navigable space
confounds.detail: An agent may slide along an obstacle and appear to take a straight-line path through a wall, producing an apparently favorable path despite behavior that would fail on a physical robot.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The Habitat challenge configures Habitat-Sim to disable sliding on collisions.

datasets.name: ALFRED
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated in AI2-THOR on seen and unseen validation/test folds; test runs use the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss. Test has 1,533 seen and 1,529 unseen annotations; the paper does not specify the number of evaluation episodes. Episodes terminate after more than 1,000 steps or more than 10 failed actions. Reports Task Success, Goal-Condition Success, and their path-weighted versions. For sub-goal evaluation, the expert trajectory forces the agent through the episode prefix before the model attempts the next sub-goal. Actions use the paper's discretized action space; interaction actions predict pixelwise masks.

Follower success during data validation means reaching within 3 m of the final panorama.

confounds.detail: The paper notes that strong VLN performance can arise from agents exploiting path biases or simply seeking the goal rather than adhering to instructions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: RxR paths are designed to reduce these biases; the paper evaluates simple go-straight baselines and compares multimodal, language-only, and vision-only agents. The multimodal agent outperforms both unimodal conditions, and go-straight baselines are less effective on RxR than on R2R.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Train: 14,025 instructions; val seen: 1,020 instructions across the same 61 scenes; val unseen: 2,349 instructions across 11 scenes; test: 4,173 instructions across 18 scenes. Test submission is trained on all training and validation data. Success is final-position shortest-path distance to the goal below 3 m; navigation error, success, oracle success, and trajectory length are reported. Text is lowercased, tokenized on whitespace, and words occurring fewer than five times are filtered.

confounds.name: Success may reflect the agent's stopping decision, not just recognition of the goal location

confounds.ruled_out_by: Also report success under oracle stopping, where the agent stops at the closest point to the goal on its trajectory.

confounds.name: The LAW advantage may occur only when the language-aligned and shortest paths are similar
confounds.detail: If gains were limited to episodes where the two paths coincide closely, they would not support the claim that language-aligned supervision helps when goal-oriented supervision is misaligned with the instruction.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper groups episodes by nDTW similarity between the reference language-aligned path and the shortest path, and reports that LAW performs better especially in the lower-similarity groups.

confounds.name: Similar performance across waypoint densities may be because the R2R trajectories are short, making LAW pano denser than necessary
confounds.detail: If short trajectories make pano waypoint supervision effectively dense enough, similar results across densities would not show that different waypoint densities are generally equivalent.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors inspect FG-R2R sub-instruction-to-waypoint mappings, find that a sub-instruction often maps to several pano waypoints, and report that LAW#4 is better than LAW pano for such paths.

evidence_standards.name: 95% confidence-interval error bars

controls.name: Random agent
controls.detail: Selects actions according to the training-set action distribution: 68% forward, 15% turn-left, 15% turn-right, and 2% stop.
controls.rules_out: That the learned agents’ performance is explained by chance action selection alone.

controls.name: Hand-crafted agent
controls.detail: Chooses a random heading, takes 37 forward actions, then stops.
controls.rules_out: That the learned agents’ performance is explained by this simple heading-and-forward trajectory heuristic.

controls.name: No Image ablation
controls.detail: Removes RGB input while retaining depth, instruction, and history.
controls.rules_out: That the full model’s result requires no RGB input.

controls.name: No Depth ablation
controls.detail: Removes depth input while retaining RGB, instruction, and history.
controls.rules_out: That the full model’s result requires no depth input.

controls.name: No Vision ablation
controls.detail: Removes visual input while retaining instruction and history.
controls.rules_out: That the full model’s result can be explained without visual perception.

controls.name: No Instruction ablation
controls.detail: Removes instruction input while retaining RGBD and history.
controls.rules_out: That the full model’s result can be explained without language instructions.

controls.name: Training-technique ablations
controls.detail: Compare Progress Monitor, DAgger, and synthetic Data Augmentation individually and in combinations against the standard training condition for both model architectures.
controls.rules_out: That performance differences for the combined training setup are attributable to any one technique without comparing conditions that omit or combine the techniques.

confounds.name: The VLN-to-VLN-CE performance gap reflects differences in trajectory coverage or path conversion, rather than the nav-graph prior
confounds.detail: Some R2R trajectories cannot be navigated in the continuous reconstructions, and continuous paths can translate poorly to sparse nav-graph trajectories.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors note that about 20% of VLN trajectories are non-navigable and excluded, and estimate these effects account for about 10 SPL when comparing VLN-CE validation results with converted-path results; they report that a substantial gap remains.

confounds.name: The Progress Monitor’s poorer results without augmentation reflect overfitting rather than the loss being ineffective
confounds.detail: The auxiliary loss may hurt generalization because it overfits the non-augmented training data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare val-unseen progress-monitor loss: 0.67 without data augmentation versus 0.47 with augmentation.

datasets.name: R2R
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on validation seen, validation unseen, and test unseen splits. Results are reported in greedy single-instruction and multiple-instruction settings. Reports TL, NE, SR, and SPL; SPL is the primary metric and the others are auxiliary. The dataset pairs each of 7,189 trajectories with three instructions.

datasets.name: CVDN
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on validation unseen and test unseen environments. Reports Goal Progress under Oracle (shortest-path), Navigator, and Mixed supervision paths; Mixed uses the navigator path when available and otherwise the shortest path.

datasets.name: HANNA
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports results on the test splits SEEN-ENV and UNSEEN-ALL using SR, SPL, NE, and number of requests (#R).

baselines.name: PreSS
baselines.fair_comparison: For the multiple-instruction comparison, the paper follows PreSS and reports Prevalent results in that setting.

baselines.name: BERT pre-training
baselines.fair_comparison: BERT is pretrained with the original MLM loss on the paper's R2R pre-training dataset, then fine-tuned on CVDN.

baselines.name: BERT fine-tuning
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper directly fine-tunes off-the-shelf BERT on CVDN.

baselines.name: Perfect assistance
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the teacher navigation policy to make decisions while executing an assistant subtask.

controls.name: MLM-only pre-training ablation
controls.detail: Pretrains with the masked-language-modeling loss but removes the action-prediction loss; compared with the full action-prediction-plus-MLM objective on CVDN.
controls.rules_out: Improvement being attributable to MLM alone rather than the added action-prediction objective.

confounds.name: Action-prediction gains are explained by MLM alone
confounds.detail: The apparent benefit of the full pre-training objective could occur even if adding action prediction contributes nothing beyond masked language modeling.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare the full action-prediction-plus-MLM objective with MLM-only pre-training on CVDN using Goal Progress across Navigation QA, Oracle Answer, and All inputs.

confounds.name: Image-attended learning is unnecessary; generic BERT pre-training or fine-tuning suffices
confounds.detail: The gains could come from generic language-model pre-training or fine-tuning rather than grounding masked-word learning in image information.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare CVDN Goal Progress for Prevalent variants with BERT pretrained using the original MLM loss on the R2R pre-training data and with off-the-shelf BERT fine-tuned on CVDN.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Human wayfinding uses trajectories from val-seen (340) and val-unseen (783); each instruction is followed by three different annotators. The compatibility-model classification task uses val-unseen (3,915 instructions) for validation and val-seen (1,700) for test, with AUC scoring. Correlation analyses use R2R val-seen and val-unseen instructions and reference instructions where required. For data augmentation, the model ranks 170k Speaker-Follower instruction-trajectory pairs; agents trained on ranked fractions are compared with agents trained on random samples of the same size and evaluated on val-unseen. For compatibility-model training, the paper uses R2R train (4,675 trajectories; 14k original positive pairs), expands positives by round-trip translation through ten languages, and filters paraphrases to BLEU [0.25, 0.7] against the original.

baselines.name: Speaker-Follower
baselines.fair_comparison: Its authors provided generated instructions for the same R2R val-seen and val-unseen trajectories used in the human evaluation; each instruction was evaluated by three wayfinders. The model was trained on R2R train.

baselines.name: EnvDrop
baselines.fair_comparison: Its authors provided generated instructions for the same R2R val-seen and val-unseen trajectories used in the human evaluation; each instruction was evaluated by three wayfinders. The model was trained on R2R train.

baselines.name: Crafty
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same val-seen trajectories and by three wayfinders per instruction. The paper notes Crafty has access to ground-truth object annotations, unlike the learned generators.

baselines.name: Human instructions
baselines.fair_comparison: 340 newly collected instructions for R2R val-seen trajectories, evaluated by three wayfinders per instruction.

baselines.name: Huang et al. (2019) compatibility model
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper’s R2R instruction-classification validation and test sets using AUC; the paper does not specify further matching of training conditions.

metrics.name: Success weighted by inverse Path Length (SPL)
Success weighted by normalized Dynamic Time Warping (SDTW)
Visual Search cost
metrics.caveat: People may succeed with poor instructions by expending additional effort; the paper also reports visual search cost, time, and subjective instruction quality.

metrics.name: Time
metrics.caveat: Time correlates with instruction length and may be affected by wayfinders giving up on poor instructions; the paper reports it alongside wayfinding outcomes and other effort/quality measures.

metrics.name: BLEU-4
metrics.caveat: The paper finds standard text metrics including BLEU ineffective for grounded navigation instructions; it compares them with human wayfinding outcomes and recommends SPICE for system-level evaluation when references are available.

metrics.name: CIDEr
metrics.caveat: The paper finds standard text metrics including CIDEr ineffective for grounded navigation instructions; it compares them with human wayfinding outcomes and recommends SPICE for system-level evaluation when references are available.

metrics.name: METEOR
metrics.caveat: The paper finds standard text metrics including METEOR ineffective for grounded navigation instructions; it compares them with human wayfinding outcomes and recommends SPICE for system-level evaluation when references are available.

metrics.name: ROUGE
metrics.caveat: The paper finds standard text metrics including ROUGE ineffective for grounded navigation instructions; it compares them with human wayfinding outcomes and recommends SPICE for system-level evaluation when references are available.

metrics.name: SPICE
metrics.caveat: It correlates with human outcomes at the system level, but individual-instruction SPICE scores have high variance and do not correlate with wayfinder performance; the paper recommends the compatibility model for individual instructions.

metrics.name: BERTScore
metrics.caveat: Compared against human outcomes; it is less correlated than the compatibility score for individual instructions, especially on model-generated instructions.

metrics.name: VLN agent-based SPL/SDTW scores
metrics.caveat: System-level correlations are unreliable for the evaluated out-of-domain styles; the paper also reports instance-level results and compares them with compatibility scores.

metrics.name: Kendall’s tau
metrics.caveat: Correlation intervals are wide for system-level comparisons; the paper reports instance-level results as well and gives 90% bootstrap confidence intervals.

metrics.name: Instruction-trajectory compatibility score
metrics.caveat: It does not reliably rank out-of-domain systems at the system level; the paper reports that it correlates most closely with human wayfinding outcomes when scoring individual instructions.

controls.name: Direction Swap human-instruction perturbation
controls.detail: Human instructions have directional phrases randomly swapped with alternatives.
controls.rules_out: Comparison with unperturbed human instructions tests whether the wayfinding outcomes depend on direction words being correct.

controls.name: Entity Swap human-instruction perturbation
controls.detail: Human instructions have entities randomly swapped.
controls.rules_out: Comparison with unperturbed human instructions tests whether the wayfinding outcomes depend on the named entities being correct.

controls.name: Phrase Swap human-instruction perturbation
controls.detail: A subsentence is removed or duplicated, or sentences are shuffled (except the last).
controls.rules_out: Comparison with unperturbed human instructions tests whether the wayfinding outcomes depend on the instruction’s steps and ordering.

controls.name: Compatibility model with no perturbations
controls.detail: An ablation removes instruction and trajectory perturbations from hard-negative mining.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full model’s performance depends on using perturbed hard negatives.

controls.name: Compatibility model with instruction perturbations only
controls.detail: An ablation uses instruction perturbations but no trajectory perturbations.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether instruction perturbations alone account for the full model’s performance.

controls.name: Compatibility model with trajectory perturbations only
controls.detail: An ablation uses trajectory perturbations but no instruction perturbations.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether trajectory perturbations alone account for the full model’s performance.

controls.name: Individual hard-negative perturbation ablations
controls.detail: Separate ablations use only Direction Swap, Entity Swap, Phrase Swap, Viewpoint Swap, Random Walk, or Path Reversal.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full model’s performance depends on a single perturbation type.

controls.name: Random augmented-data fractions
controls.detail: VLN agents are trained on random samples of augmented pairs matched in size to compatibility-model-ranked fractions.
controls.rules_out: Rules out the gain being explained merely by using a particular fraction of augmented data.

controls.name: Loss-function ablations
controls.detail: The paper compares classification losses (cross-entropy or focal) and contrastive-loss combinations.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the reported compatibility-model gains depend on the proposed combination of losses.

confounds.name: Wayfinders compensate for poor instructions through extra effort
confounds.detail: A poor instruction could still produce successful navigation if people spend more effort searching, making success alone overstate instruction quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper additionally measures visual search cost, task time, and subjective instruction quality.

confounds.name: Annotator adaptation over time
confounds.detail: Wayfinding performance could change as annotators learn the task, rather than reflect instruction quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors report that annotator performance stays consistent over time and shows no sign of adaptation.

confounds.name: Out-of-domain style mismatch in system-level metric comparisons
confounds.detail: The model-based evaluators may fail to rank systems because their styles differ from the R2R data used to train them, rather than because the scores lack validity in general.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors identify the varied styles and training-data mismatch as a limitation and report that the model-based approaches do not reliably rank these out-of-domain systems.

evidence_standards.name: Human wayfinding ratings
evidence_standards.detail: Each instruction is evaluated by three different wayfinders; the study reports 11,886 attempts using 37 English-speaking annotators.

evidence_standards.name: Correlation uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Kendall’s tau results are reported with 90% confidence intervals based on bootstrap resampling.

evidence_standards.name: VLN-agent data-augmentation comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Results are means over three runs, with standard deviation shown as error bars.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the Validation Unseen set in Matterport3D; reports SR, SPL, SED, CLS, nDTW, and SDTW as percentages. No evaluation episode count or preprocessing is stated.

datasets.name: Room-for-Room (R4R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the Validation Unseen set in Matterport3D; reports SR, SPL, SED, CLS, nDTW, and SDTW as percentages. No evaluation episode count or preprocessing is stated.

baselines.name: random agent
baselines.fair_comparison: Step count is sampled from the reference-path-length distribution; each step uniformly samples among possible neighbors, and scores are averaged over one million random trajectories.

metrics.name: Success Rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: On R4R, it does not differentiate between goal-oriented and fidelity-oriented agents; SDTW is reported to capture both success and fidelity.

metrics.name: Success weighted by Path Length (SPL)
metrics.caveat: Its apparent distinction between goal-oriented and fidelity-oriented agents on R4R (15.0 vs. 21.4) is attributed only to the fidelity-oriented agent producing paths closer in length to the references, not to greater path fidelity; nDTW and SDTW are also reported.

metrics.name: Success weighted by Edit Distance (SED)
metrics.caveat: On R4R, it scores random paths higher than trained agents and does not differentiate between goal-oriented and fidelity-oriented agents; SDTW is also reported.

metrics.name: Coverage weighted by Length Score (CLS)
metrics.caveat: On R4R, nDTW differentiates the goal-oriented and fidelity-oriented agents better; both metrics are reported.

metrics.name: Success weighted by normalized Dynamic Time Warping (SDTW)

controls.name: goal-oriented reward condition
controls.detail: The comparison agent receives goal-distance progress rewards and an episode completion reward, rather than the fidelity-oriented agent's nDTW progress reward and navigation-error-based terminal reward.
controls.rules_out: That the reported improvement over this comparison is due merely to training an agent with a reward signal, rather than using the nDTW-based fidelity reward.

confounds.name: SPL improvement reflects reference-path length similarity rather than path fidelity
confounds.detail: The fidelity-oriented agent scores higher on SPL, but that result could occur because its paths have lengths more similar to the reference paths, without being more faithful to them.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper also reports nDTW and SDTW, on which the fidelity-oriented agent outperforms the goal-oriented agent; it identifies SDTW as the clearest signal of both success and fidelity.

evidence_standards.name: Human-ranking comparison uses a sign test
evidence_standards.detail: For each human ranking, the authors assign a positive or negative sign according to which metric has higher correlation, discard ties, and compare across reference paths with a binomial sign test under the null p=0.5; p-values are reported.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation involved 9 raters
evidence_standards.detail: The study collected annotations on 2,525 samples (505 sets of five path pairs), split into 1,325 unconstrained and 1,200 success-constrained samples.

evidence_standards.name: Random-baseline estimate averages one million trajectories
evidence_standards.detail: The random agent's scores are averaged over one million randomly generated trajectories.

datasets.name: R2R
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on Val Seen, Val Unseen, and Test Unseen splits; reports Navigation Error (NE), Success Rate (SR), and SPL. No episode count or additional evaluation preprocessing is specified. Panoramic observations contain 36 images.

datasets.name: CVDN
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on Val Seen, Val Unseen, and Test Unseen splits; reports Goal Progress (GP). State-of-the-art comparison uses the whole dialog history; results are reported for Oracle, Navigator, and Mixed supervision settings. Ablations also evaluate Last A, Last QA, and All dialog-history settings. No episode count is specified.

baselines.name: EnvDrop
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper says its navigator architecture, training hyperparameters, and training strategy are the same as [7] (EnvDrop).

baselines.name: Static attack
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an attack mechanism and in adversarial training on CVDN; uses the pretrained DR-Attacker's first-timestep prediction, then keeps the same substitution at each timestep.

baselines.name: Random attack
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an attack mechanism and in adversarial training on CVDN; randomly selects the target word and substitution word at each timestep.

baselines.name: Heuristics attack
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an attack mechanism and in adversarial training on CVDN; attacks the word with the navigator's highest textual attention at each timestep.

baselines.name: PWWS
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an attack mechanism and in adversarial training on CVDN; uses change in action-prediction probability as the attack objective in place of classification probability.

metrics.name: Success rate weighted by Path Length (SPL)

controls.name: Base Agent
controls.detail: Navigator trained on original instructions (with the paper's specified training setup); used as the reference in ablations.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether the reported adversarial-training and finetuning conditions improve on the unmodified training condition.

controls.name: Adversarial training without the auxiliary reasoning task
controls.detail: Table VI compares finetuning after adversarial training without the auxiliary self-supervised reasoning task against finetuning with that task.
controls.rules_out: A difference isolates the contribution of the auxiliary reasoning task from adversarial training alone.

controls.name: Random attack
controls.detail: Randomly selects the target word and candidate substitution word at each timestep; evaluated as an attack and in adversarial training.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether results require DR-Attacker's learned selection rather than arbitrary word substitutions.

controls.name: Static attack
controls.detail: Uses the pretrained DR-Attacker's first-timestep word prediction and applies the same substitution at every timestep.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the reported advantage requires timestep-varying attacks rather than a fixed perturbation.
