datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on seen and unseen validation splits and the unseen test split. For each instruction, beam search with the follower model from [28] produces up to 30 candidate paths; over 99% of candidate sets contain a path reaching the goal. The model selects one path from each set. Success is ending within 3 m of the goal. Path-selection metrics use only the selected path; leaderboard results prepend the exploration path, affecting path-length-based metrics.

baselines.name: follower [28]
baselines.fair_comparison: On path selection, evaluated using the same candidate paths generated by beam search with the follower; the follower selects the top beam.

baselines.name: speaker [28]
baselines.fair_comparison: On path selection, evaluated using the same candidate paths generated by beam search with the follower.

baselines.name: speaker + follower [28]
baselines.fair_comparison: Ensemble weights are selected by grid search on the R2R unseen validation split.

baselines.name: speaker + follower + follower
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same candidate paths; ensemble weights are selected by grid search on the unseen validation split.

baselines.name: speaker + follower + speaker
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same candidate paths; ensemble weights are selected by grid search on the unseen validation split.

metrics.name: Path length (PL)
metrics.caveat: A lower path length is preferred if the trajectory is successful; SR is reported alongside it.

metrics.name: Success rate weighted by path length (SPL)

controls.name: No-pretraining ablation
controls.detail: VLN-BERT is trained without any of the three pretraining stages.
controls.rules_out: A comparison with the full curriculum measures whether the curriculum improves over training the model from scratch.

controls.name: Language-only pretraining ablation
controls.detail: Uses the language stage but omits visual grounding and action grounding.
controls.rules_out: A comparison with the full curriculum tests whether the full result is explained by language pretraining alone.

controls.name: Language plus visual grounding; no action grounding
controls.detail: Uses the language and Conceptual Captions visual-grounding stages but omits action grounding.
controls.rules_out: A comparison with the full curriculum tests whether action grounding adds benefit beyond the earlier stages.

controls.name: Language plus action grounding; no visual grounding
controls.detail: Uses language and action grounding but skips the Conceptual Captions visual-grounding stage.
controls.rules_out: A comparison with the full curriculum tests whether its gains require the web image-text visual-grounding stage.

controls.name: Speaker + follower + an additional speaker or follower
controls.detail: The paper adds a randomly seeded speaker or follower to the speaker-plus-follower ensemble, matching the three-model ensemble size.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the improvement from adding VLN-BERT is merely the generic benefit of adding a third model.

confounds.name: The gains could come from language or action pretraining rather than web visual grounding
confounds.detail: Higher path-selection performance alone would not show that image-text pretraining contributes to embodied visual grounding.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The curriculum ablations compare the full curriculum with one omitting visual grounding; the paper reports a 9-point unseen-validation SR drop when visual grounding is skipped.

confounds.name: The model's score changes may not reflect grounding instruction phrases in relevant image regions
confounds.detail: A performance gain could occur even if the model does not base compatibility scores on the visually relevant regions referenced by the instruction.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper qualitatively measures region-feature gradients and compares region importance before and after removing instruction phrases; it reports importance shifting away from regions for the removed reference and toward other relevant regions.

datasets.name: R2R
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports single-run results on Val Seen, Val Unseen, and Test Unseen. Reports TL, NE, OSR, SR, and SPL; SR counts paths with NE < 3 m. Also evaluates training-data amounts of 10%, 50%, and 100% on Val Seen and Val Unseen.

datasets.name: RxR
datasets.eval_protocol: Zero-shot evaluation on the English unseen split; reports nDTW, sDTW, OSR, SR, and SPL.

datasets.name: HM3D
datasets.eval_protocol: Zero-shot evaluation on 1,000 trajectories sampled from ScaleVLN, using Habitat Simulator-rendered images; reports TL, NE, OSR, SR, and SPL.

baselines.name: DUET
baselines.fair_comparison: For the comparison at the same MP3D training scale, the paper compares against the original DUET.

baselines.name: DUET (w/o local branch)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same action-planning policy architecture and amount of training data as NavGPT-2; the language branch differs, using a 12-layer transformer initialized from LXMERT instead of LLM latents.

metrics.name: Success weighted by Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (SDTW)

controls.name: DUET (w/o local branch; LXMERT language branch)
controls.detail: The paper's constructed baseline uses the same action-planning policy architecture and training-data amount as NavGPT-2, but replaces the LLM-latent language branch with a 12-layer LXMERT-initialized transformer.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference explained simply by training-data amount or action-policy architecture rather than the language representation.

controls.name: NavGPT-2 without the policy model
controls.detail: Removes visual-language cross-attention layers in the Q-former and policy network, leaving a graph-aware self-attention layer and feed-forward action predictor.
controls.rules_out: That NavGPT-2's navigation performance is achieved without the navigation-specific policy model.

controls.name: NavGPT-2 without pretrained Q-former for reasoning
controls.detail: Ablates pretraining the Q-former on navigational reasoning data.
controls.rules_out: That the reported effect of reasoning pretraining is present when that pretraining is removed.

confounds.name: The gain could come from more training data or a different action-planning policy, rather than the LLM-latent language branch
confounds.detail: The headline comparison could look better even if the language representation were not responsible, if NavGPT-2 simply had more training data or a stronger/different policy architecture.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare with the constructed DUET (w/o local branch) baseline, which uses the same policy architecture and training-data amount but a 12-layer LXMERT-initialized language branch.

evidence_standards.name: Single-run R2R comparison
evidence_standards.detail: The paper explicitly reports single-run performance; it does not state a seed count, uncertainty interval, statistical test, or threshold for treating results as ties.

evidence_standards.name: Human study of generated navigational reasoning
evidence_standards.detail: 10 volunteers rated 30 held-out samples for accuracy, informativeness, and rationality on scales from 0 to 3.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on Validation Seen (1,021 samples) and Validation Unseen (2,249 samples); reports PL, NE, SR, SPL, and CLS. Validation Seen uses environments overlapping training; Validation Unseen uses disjoint environments.

datasets.name: Room-for-Room (R4R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on Validation Seen (1,035 samples) and Validation Unseen (4,516 samples); reports PL, NE, SR, SPL, and CLS. R4R paths are formed by joining R2R paths whose endpoints are within a distance threshold, with their instructions combined.

baselines.name: Random
baselines.fair_comparison: For each trajectory, sample its number of edges from the training reference-path edge-count distribution, then uniformly sample a neighboring node at each step; report average metrics over 1 million trajectories.

baselines.name: Speaker-Follower (Fried et al., 2018)
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported with panoramic action space and augmented data, but without beam search (pragmatic inference).

baselines.name: RCM (Wang et al., 2019)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper reports the RCM benchmark without intrinsic reward; it notes its own goal-oriented results match that benchmark on Validation Unseen but are lower on Validation Seen, possibly because of implementation details and hyperparameters.

metrics.name: NE (Navigation Error)
metrics.caveat: Measures distance to the final reference node, not conformity to the intervening reference path; CLS is reported alongside it.

metrics.name: SR (Success Rate)
metrics.caveat: Measures reaching the goal within a threshold and does not measure path fidelity; CLS is reported alongside it.

metrics.name: SPL (Success weighted by Path Length)
metrics.caveat: Can be misleading for twisty paths, especially when start and end locations are close, because it assumes the shortest distance between them is the optimal path; CLS is reported alongside it.

controls.name: Goal-oriented reward
controls.detail: An RCM condition rewarded for reaching the target, without the fidelity-oriented CLS reward; compared with the fidelity-oriented reward condition.
controls.rules_out: That the fidelity-oriented result is explained merely by training to reach the goal; a difference supports the contribution of the fidelity reward.

controls.name: Partial or absent instructions
controls.detail: Evaluate agents trained with full instructions using only the last five tokens or no instructions.
controls.rules_out: Whether performance depends on receiving the full instruction rather than only visual input or a short instruction fragment.

controls.name: Arbitrary validation instructions
controls.detail: Give the agent an arbitrary instruction from the validation set while leaving the reference path unchanged.
controls.rules_out: Whether the no-instruction result is merely caused by distribution shift or changed instruction length.

confounds.name: Navigation success comes from environmental biases or goal-seeking shortcuts rather than following language
confounds.detail: An agent could reach the target using scene or environment structure while largely ignoring the instructions, producing good goal metrics without instruction fidelity.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate with no instructions, with only the last five tokens, and with arbitrary instructions while keeping the reference path fixed; compare CLS, including on R4R.

confounds.name: Instruction-removal results reflect distribution shift rather than lack of language reliance
confounds.detail: Removing instructions changes the evaluation input distribution, which could itself explain a performance change.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate with arbitrary validation instructions while keeping the reference path unchanged; the paper reports results similar to the no-instruction condition.

datasets.name: R2R
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on validation-seen, validation-unseen, and test-unseen splits; report single-run results, selecting the model with the highest validation-unseen SR. Report TL, NE, SR, and SPL; SR and SPL on unseen environments are the main metrics. Use ResNet-152 features pretrained on Places365 and Faster-RCNN object detections encoded with GloVe; retain the top 100 object classes from R2R training data, with 4 neighbor views and 8 objects per neighbor by default. Train in two stages: real training data, then real plus synthetic data.

datasets.name: R4R
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on validation-seen and validation-unseen splits; report single-run results, selecting the model with the highest validation-unseen SR. Report NE, SR, SPL, CLS, nDTW, and sDTW; the paper distinguishes SR/SPL as navigation accuracy metrics and CLS/nDTW/sDTW as path-fidelity metrics. Use the same default features and 4-neighbor/8-object setting as R2R; train using only the first training stage.

metrics.name: SR (Success Rate)
metrics.caveat: The paper defines SR as success at stopping within 3 meters of the target. For R4R, it distinguishes SR as measuring navigation accuracy from CLS, nDTW, and sDTW, which measure path fidelity.

metrics.name: SPL (Success Rate weighted by Path Length)
metrics.caveat: The paper says SPL considers both path length and success rate. For R4R, it distinguishes SPL as measuring navigation accuracy from CLS, nDTW, and sDTW, which measure path fidelity.

metrics.name: CLS (Coverage Weighted by Length Score)
metrics.caveat: The paper groups CLS with path-fidelity metrics, alongside nDTW and sDTW, rather than the navigation-accuracy metrics SR and SPL.

metrics.name: nDTW (Normalized Dynamic Time Warping)
metrics.caveat: The paper groups nDTW with path-fidelity metrics, alongside CLS and sDTW, rather than the navigation-accuracy metrics SR and SPL.

metrics.name: sDTW (nDTW weighted by Success Rate)
metrics.caveat: The paper groups sDTW with path-fidelity metrics, alongside CLS and nDTW, rather than the navigation-accuracy metrics SR and SPL.

controls.name: NvEM without the action module
controls.detail: Ablation removes the module that uses candidate orientation and action-related phrases; subject and reference modules remain.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full-model result depends on the action module rather than the other modules alone.

controls.name: NvEM without the subject module
controls.detail: Ablation removes the subject module that aggregates neighbor views globally; action and reference modules remain.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full-model result depends on the subject module rather than the other modules alone.

controls.name: NvEM without the reference module
controls.detail: Ablation removes the reference module that aggregates neighbor objects locally; action and subject modules remain.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full-model result depends on the reference module rather than the other modules alone.

controls.name: Single-view subject module
controls.detail: In the subject-module comparison, represents the subject with single-view global features instead of neighbor-view aggregation; the reference module is removed in these comparisons.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the neighbor-view subject representation improves over a single-view representation.

controls.name: Language-grounded neighbor-view subject module
controls.detail: Uses subject-aware language phrases as the query to aggregate neighbor views; the reference module is removed in these comparisons.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the reported neighbor-view benefit is specific to the paper's spatial-affinity aggregation rather than another neighbor-view fusion method.

controls.name: Alternative neighbor-view and object counts
controls.detail: Compares 4 versus 8 neighbor views and 4, 8, or 12 detected objects per view; the default is 4 views and 8 objects.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the reported result depends on the chosen number of neighbors or objects.

confounds.name: The benefit may come from adding neighbor views, not from the paper's spatial-affinity aggregation
confounds.detail: A gain over single-view representations could be explained simply by using more views, or by a different way of fusing those views.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The subject-module ablation compares single-view features, language-grounded neighbor-view aggregation, and the paper's spatial-affinity aggregation; the spatial-affinity version performs best in the reported comparison.

confounds.name: Phrase attention can select the wrong instruction phrase and lead to an incorrect action
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that NvEM's attentive phrases are not always correct, so results may depend on phrase extraction succeeding rather than neighbor-view context alone.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The paper presents a qualitative failure visualization in which focus on “bathroom” in the subject module leads to a wrong direction.

evidence_standards.name: Single-run results
evidence_standards.detail: The state-of-the-art comparisons are explicitly reported under a single-run setting; the paper does not report multiple seeds, variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

evidence_standards.name: Validation-unseen checkpoint selection
evidence_standards.detail: Reported performance is for the model with the highest SR on the validation-unseen split.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the validation seen and unseen splits using NE, SR (stop within 3 m of the goal), OSR (reach within 3 m with a view of the goal), and SPL. Low-data experiments use 10 training trajectories sampled from one scene or 100 from two scenes; the synthetic-data experiments generally use image captions only, while the ALFRED-to-R2R transfer experiments use object information. Evaluation episode count is not stated.

baselines.name: GPT-4 (zero-shot)
baselines.fair_comparison: Prompted to complete trajectories using the navigation template; no few-shot demonstration.

baselines.name: GPT-4 (few-shot)
baselines.fair_comparison: Prompted with one full navigation trajectory as a demonstration, due to context-length limits.

baselines.name: NavGPT
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same GPT-4 backbone; the paper notes NavGPT additionally uses ground-truth distance information and chain-of-thought prompting.

baselines.name: RecBert
baselines.fair_comparison: Finetuning methods use the same 10 or 100 R2R trajectories. In the domain-transfer experiments, RecBert and LangNav are compared with matching R2R finetuning amounts and pretraining conditions.

baselines.name: DuET
baselines.fair_comparison: Finetuning methods use the same 10 or 100 R2R trajectories.

baselines.name: LLaMA2-7B finetuned on real trajectories only
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same 10 or 100 real trajectories as the other finetuning methods, without the synthetic trajectories.

metrics.name: Success weighted by the normalized inverse of the Path Length (SPL)

controls.name: LLaMA2-7B finetuned on real trajectories only
controls.detail: Finetune on the same 10 or 100 real R2R trajectories, omitting the 10,000 GPT-4-generated trajectories used by the main synthetic-data condition.
controls.rules_out: That the gains over the seed-data setting come merely from finetuning on the real seed trajectories.

controls.name: Vision-only RecBert
controls.detail: Compare RecBert using ResNet visual features alone with the version that concatenates BERT caption representations to those features.
controls.rules_out: That the vision-plus-language gains require no language representation; the comparison tests the contribution of adding language features.

controls.name: Caption-only perception (no object detector)
controls.detail: Compare using image captions alone with using the object-detection module as well; the paper reports no significant performance differences and uses captions alone for those experiments.
controls.rules_out: That the reported performance in those experiments depends on the object-detection module.

confounds.name: GPT-4 may have encountered R2R instructions during pretraining
confounds.detail: If GPT-4 had seen the R2R instruction text, apparent success of its generated synthetic data might partly reflect data contamination rather than the proposed generation approach.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors check the 10,000 generated instructions and report finding none that occur in the actual R2R dataset. They say they cannot entirely rule out exposure to the text instructions, while judging exposure to the trajectories unlikely because the trajectories use vision-system captions and objects.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding
evidence_standards.detail: The LangNav action is generated by greedy decoding from the language model distribution. The paper does not state a statistical test, confidence interval, seed-based variance rule, or threshold for deciding that differences are real.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on validation-seen (1,020 instructions), validation-unseen (2,349), and test-unseen (4,173); scores are computed over evaluation instructions. Uses the panoramic action-space setting and greedy inference. Reports NE, SR, and SPL; SR uses a 3 m success threshold. The paper describes globally averaged pre-trained ResNet-152 image features, projected from 2,048 to 512 dimensions, and environmental dropout of 0.4.

baselines.name: Seq2Seq
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison.

baselines.name: RPA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison.

baselines.name: Speaker-Follower
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison. In the AAL integration comparison, all methods are trained without data augmentation.

baselines.name: RCM
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison. Also compared under the separately reported pre-exploration setting.

baselines.name: Self-Monitoring
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison. In the AAL integration comparison, all methods are trained without data augmentation.

baselines.name: Regretful
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison.

baselines.name: FAST
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison.

baselines.name: ALTR
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison.

baselines.name: EnvDrop
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison. Also compared under the separately reported pre-exploration setting.

baselines.name: PRESS
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses PRESS results under the single-instruction setting, rather than its multiple-instruction setting, for comparison with the other methods.

baselines.name: AuxRN
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the panoramic action-space setting; the paper excludes methods relying on extra large-scale pre-training from its state-of-the-art comparison.

metrics.name: Success Rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: Does not account for trajectory length; the paper also reports SPL, which evaluates success against trajectory length.

metrics.name: Success rate weighted by (normalized inverse) Path Length (SPL)

controls.name: Teacher-forced agent
controls.detail: Same model structure as the proposed agent, trained with teacher-forcing; evaluated alongside the proposed method in the ablations.
controls.rules_out: Shows the result is not simply the outcome of teacher-forced training.

controls.name: Student-forced agent
controls.detail: Same model structure as the proposed agent, trained with student-forcing; evaluated alongside the proposed method in the ablations.
controls.rules_out: Shows the result is not simply the outcome of student-forced training.

controls.name: Professor-Forcing
controls.detail: A closely related learning-scheme comparison in the validation-set ablations.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the result follows from using the related Professor-Forcing scheme instead of the paper's proposed training approach.

controls.name: CMG + Alternate Learning
controls.detail: Removes adversarial learning while retaining the cross-modal grounding module and alternate learning.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the result requires the adversarial component, rather than alternate learning with CMG alone.

controls.name: Historical Co-grounding + Alternate Learning
controls.detail: Uses historical co-grounding with alternate learning, without mutual co-grounding or adversarial learning.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full result requires both grounding components and adversarial learning.

controls.name: Mutual Co-grounding + Alternate Learning
controls.detail: Uses mutual co-grounding with alternate learning, without historical co-grounding or adversarial learning.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full result requires both grounding components and adversarial learning.

controls.name: Historical Co-grounding + AAL
controls.detail: Uses AAL with historical co-grounding only.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full result requires the mutual co-grounding component.

controls.name: Mutual Co-grounding + AAL
controls.detail: Uses AAL with mutual co-grounding only.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full result requires the historical co-grounding component.

controls.name: Speaker-Follower without AAL
controls.detail: Compared with Speaker-Follower + AAL on validation-unseen; both were trained without data augmentation.
controls.rules_out: Provides the unmodified reference condition for measuring the effect of adding AAL to Speaker-Follower.

controls.name: Self-Monitoring without AAL
controls.detail: Compared with Self-Monitoring + AAL on validation-unseen; both were trained without data augmentation.
controls.rules_out: Provides the unmodified reference condition for measuring the effect of adding AAL to Self-Monitoring.

confounds.name: The comparison could be inflated by extra large-scale pre-training data
confounds.detail: The paper notes that extra large-scale pre-training consistently boosts performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For the state-of-the-art comparison, it compares against VLN agents that do not rely on extra large-scale pre-training.

confounds.name: PRESS's multiple-instruction setting could explain its reported performance
confounds.detail: Aggregating multiple instructions for the same trajectory boosts performance and would make the comparison unlike the other methods.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports PRESS under the single-instruction setting for the comparison.

confounds.name: AAL's gains on existing baselines could be due to data augmentation
confounds.detail: Data augmentation could contribute to the improvement attributed to adding AAL.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The Speaker-Follower and Self-Monitoring comparisons with and without AAL are all trained without data augmentation.

confounds.name: AAL's improvement could be specific to one underlying navigator
confounds.detail: The gain might reflect the original navigator rather than a training strategy that generalizes across models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Integrates AAL with both Speaker-Follower and Self-Monitoring and reports results for each.

confounds.name: Differences in software, GPU type, and hyperparameters affect the external-baseline comparison
confounds.detail: The paper acknowledges that its Speaker-Follower and Self-Monitoring results differ from their original reported numbers for these reasons.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper reports these differences as a qualification on the comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding at inference
evidence_standards.detail: The agent selects the action with the highest predicted probability. The paper does not report seeds, variance estimates, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: Matterport3D (MP3D)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated in Habitat using the standard 56-scene train / 11-scene validation split; the held-out challenge test set is not used. Navigation evaluation uses 2,480 episodes across validation scenes, random starts in scenes unseen during map-predictor training, 11 object-goal categories, and a 500-step budget. An episode succeeds when the agent stops within 1 m of the target. The agent receives RGB-D observations and noiseless simulator pose. The SemExp comparison uses six categories and is rerun on the paper's evaluation episodes. Map prediction is evaluated on 17,900 examples from the 11 validation scenes, using 64×64 map crops collected in sequences of length 10; it reports IoU and F1 over nine classes. Error analysis uses a harder subset of 795 episodes.

baselines.name: Random Walk
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper's 11-object evaluation set; no further fairness controls are stated.

baselines.name: Segm. + ANS + OracleStop
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the paper's 11-object evaluation set. It uses Active Neural SLAM for exploration and the paper's image segmentation to detect objects; an oracle decides to stop when the agent reaches the correct target.

baselines.name: SemExp
baselines.fair_comparison: The challenge model was unavailable, so the authors compare against the Mask R-CNN variant on the six object categories reported in the SemExp paper, rerunning it on their own evaluation episodes.

metrics.name: Soft SPL
metrics.caveat: Unlike SPL, which is 0 for failed episodes, Soft SPL measures distance covered toward the goal weighted by path length.

controls.name: L2M-Offline-UpperBound
controls.detail: Uses the upper-bound goal-selection strategy but does not fine-tune the map predictor with an active strategy.
controls.rules_out: A difference from L2M-Active-UpperBound supports a benefit from active fine-tuning rather than upper-bound goal selection alone.

controls.name: L2M-Entropy and L2M-BALD
controls.detail: Fine-tune the map predictor using entropy or BALD objectives instead of the paper's variance-based active-training objective.
controls.rules_out: Comparisons test whether the reported gains are specific to the chosen variance objective rather than to using these alternative active-training objectives.

controls.name: L2M-Active-Mean
controls.detail: Selects goals using the mean target-class probability without incorporating uncertainty.
controls.rules_out: A difference from L2M-Active-UpperBound tests whether incorporating uncertainty in goal selection adds value beyond mean-probability selection.

controls.name: L2M-Active-LowerBound and L2M-Active-Mixed
controls.detail: Use the lower-confidence-bound and mixed goal-selection strategies instead of the upper-confidence-bound strategy.
controls.rules_out: Comparisons test whether the upper-bound exploration/exploitation strategy performs differently from the paper's alternative goal-selection strategies.

controls.name: L2M + OracleStop
controls.detail: Replaces the model's stop decision with an oracle stop decision within the success distance of the target.
controls.rules_out: The performance difference measures how much failures are attributable to the stop-decision criterion.

controls.name: L2M + GtPath
controls.detail: Replaces the local policy with shortest paths from the Habitat simulator to the selected goals.
controls.rules_out: The performance difference measures how much failures are attributable to the local policy's ability to reach selected goals.

controls.name: L2M + GtPath + OracleStop
controls.detail: Uses both simulator shortest paths to selected goals and oracle stopping.
controls.rules_out: The comparison shows performance when both local-policy execution and stop-decision errors are addressed.

confounds.name: Failures may come from stopping outside the success radius rather than from poor navigation or goal selection
confounds.detail: The headline navigation result could be limited by an incorrect stop decision even when the agent has reached a suitable goal state.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors compare L2M with L2M + OracleStop, which raises success from 32.7% to 50.8% on the harder 795-episode subset.

confounds.name: Failures may come from the local policy being unable to reach selected goals
confounds.detail: The headline result could reflect execution failures by the local policy rather than the quality of the map predictions or selected goals.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors replace the local policy with simulator shortest paths in L2M + GtPath and compare performance; success rises from 32.7% to 50.4% on the harder subset.

confounds.name: The SemExp comparison could be affected by differences in evaluation episodes
confounds.detail: A difference from previously reported SemExp results could arise from using different test episodes rather than from method performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors run SemExp on their own evaluation episodes, while noting that the comparison uses the six categories reported in the SemExp paper.

datasets.name: R2R
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the validation unseen set (about 2.3k examples), using Success Rate: a navigation is successful when the final position is within 3 meters of the target. For instruction interventions, object tokens are identified with Stanza POS tags NOUN or PROPN; direction tokens are left, right, back, front, forward, and stop. For visual interventions, annotated object boxes are masked by filling them with the surrounding mean color, or viewpoint images are horizontally flipped. Agents are trained on the original training set and evaluated under their original experiment settings.

datasets.name: RxR-en
datasets.eval_protocol: Use only the English subset and evaluate on the validation unseen set (about 4.6k examples), using Success Rate: a navigation is successful when the final position is within 3 meters of the target. Numeric-token experiments use a subset of about 2.0k instructions containing cardinal numbers 1–20 or ordinal numbers 1st–20th. Instruction and visual interventions follow the paper’s described procedures; visual object boxes are masked by filling them with the surrounding mean color. Agents are trained on the original training set and evaluated under their original experiment settings.

datasets.name: Touchdown
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the test set (about 1.4k examples), using Task Completion: a navigation is successful if the agent stops at the target location or an adjacent node in the environment graph. Numeric-token experiments use a subset of about 1.0k instructions containing cardinal numbers 1–20 or ordinal numbers 1st–20th. Instruction interventions follow the paper’s described procedures. Agents are trained on the original training set and evaluated under their original experiment settings.

baselines.name: EnvDrop
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: FAST
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: VLN ⟳ BERT
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: PREVALENT
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: CLIP-ViL
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: VLN-HAMT
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: RCONCAT
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: ARC
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

baselines.name: VLN-Transformer
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the authors’ shared code and trained checkpoint; train on the original training set and follow the agent’s original experiment setting. Compare intervention conditions on the same evaluation data.

controls.name: Vanilla input condition
controls.detail: Evaluate the same agent with unmodified instructions and visual input alongside the intervention conditions.
controls.rules_out: Provides the unmodified reference score against which the intervention’s performance change is measured.

controls.name: Random token masking control
controls.detail: For object- and direction-token ablations, randomly mask the same number of instruction tokens as in the targeted-token masking condition.
controls.rules_out: That the performance drop is explained merely by having fewer visible instruction tokens, rather than by removing the targeted tokens.

controls.name: Random visual-object masking control
controls.detail: For foreground-object masking, mask the same number of randomly selected visible objects at the viewpoint, regardless of depth.
controls.rules_out: That the foreground-versus-background result is simply due to masking a small number of objects rather than which objects or depths are masked.

controls.name: Random visual-object control for dynamic masking
controls.detail: At each viewpoint, randomly mask the same number of visual objects as in the condition that masks objects mentioned in the instruction.
controls.rules_out: That the effect of dynamically masking instruction-mentioned objects is explained by masking that many visual objects in general.

confounds.name: Object-token masking reduces the number of visible instruction tokens
confounds.detail: A decline after masking object tokens could result from reducing the amount of visible text, rather than from the agents’ dependence on object information.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare object-token masking with a controlled trial that randomly masks the same number of tokens.

confounds.name: Visual-object ablation effects may reflect dataset, agent, or visual-feature differences
confounds.detail: Differences in results across the indoor experiments could be caused by the agent design, dataset domain, or visual feature extractor rather than the visual information being tested.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run additional object-ablation experiments with the same EnvDrop agent using ResNet-152 and CLIP-ViT features across R2R and RxR-en; the authors report that the background-information trend persists.

confounds.name: Dynamic visual masking may hurt performance through generic visual corruption rather than removal of aligned targets
confounds.detail: A decline when masking instruction-mentioned objects could occur because visual objects were removed, without the agent actually aligning those textual mentions to the masked instances.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare dynamic masking with a control that randomly masks the same number of visual objects at each viewpoint.

evidence_standards.name: Five repeated experiments for random masking or replacing
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports the average scores across five repetitive experiments for settings involving random masking or replacing. It does not report a statistical test, variance estimate, or numerical threshold for deciding that a difference is real.

datasets.name: Matterport3D (MP3D) ObjectNav
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the Habitat ObjectNav task with 21 goal categories and a 500-step episode limit; success requires stopping within 1 m of an instance and being able to view it. Reports results on val and test-std, with evaluation GPS vertical position zeroed (2D GPS). Training uses ground-truth semantic segmentation; evaluation uses RedNet-predicted segmentation, with some variants additionally fine-tuned on RedNet. Checkpoints are evaluated about every 4M frames and selected by highest SPL on val. A separate analysis evaluates 300-episode subsets of train and val with both ground-truth and RedNet segmentation.

metrics.name: Success
metrics.caveat: Does not capture trajectory efficiency; the paper reports SPL alongside it.

metrics.name: Observation–belief curvature correlation
metrics.caveat: The authors note that relatively stable computation independent of moment-to-moment observations may not show up in this measure; they also report that the CP belief is less correlated with observations than the other beliefs.

metrics.name: Fixed-point memory span
metrics.caveat: The paper measures it by counting eigenvalues whose time constants exceed a threshold; it reports rankings across beliefs and agents, as well as changes during training.

controls.name: Base agent without Action Distribution Prediction (ADP)
controls.detail: Ablates ADP from the 4-action base agent.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference against the full agent supports a contribution from ADP rather than merely adding the other auxiliary tasks.

controls.name: Base agent without Generalized Inverse Dynamics (GID)
controls.detail: Ablates GID from the 4-action base agent.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference against the full agent supports a contribution from GID rather than merely adding the other auxiliary tasks.

controls.name: Base agent without Coverage Prediction (CP)
controls.detail: Ablates CP from the 4-action base agent.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference against the full agent supports a contribution from CP rather than merely adding the other auxiliary tasks.

controls.name: Base agent without Semantic Goal Exists (SGE)
controls.detail: Removes the SGE input feature from the 4-action base agent.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference against the full agent supports a contribution from the SGE feature.

controls.name: 6-action agent with direct sparse-reward tuning
controls.detail: Fine-tunes directly on the sparse ObjectNav reward, compared with tethered-policy training.
controls.rules_out: A difference tests whether tethered training preserves performance better than simply fine-tuning on the sparse reward.

confounds.name: The apparent generalization or performance differences could reflect agent overfitting to the training environments.
confounds.detail: The headline results could look stronger or differ between agents because performance is specific to the training scenes.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates 300-episode subsets of train and val with ground-truth segmentation; reports that agents are minimally overfit in this setting, with less than a 3% success drop.

confounds.name: RedNet segmentation overfitting or instability, rather than the proposed agent behavior, explains the differences between action settings.
confounds.detail: An overfit or noisy segmentation model could transfer its errors to the agent and produce the observed performance changes.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares train and val performance with both ground-truth and RedNet segmentation and examines the effects of unstable predicted segmentation; the paper also says it quantifies segmentation-related instability in Section A.7.

confounds.name: Belief dynamics may be driven by intermediate computation rather than by observations.
confounds.detail: If so, the observed relationship between belief dynamics and input dynamics would not establish that beliefs track observations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measures the correlation between belief-trajectory curvature and observation-embedding curvature across transitions in 300 episodes.

evidence_standards.name: Validation comparisons use 95% confidence intervals and paired t-tests
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports ± intervals as 95% CIs and marks validation values as significantly better at p<0.05 using a paired t-test. Test-set bolding is for emphasis, not a stated significance test.

evidence_standards.name: Decoder analysis uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Reports 95% confidence intervals across individual beliefs for the representation probes.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on val-unseen (2,349 path-instruction pairs) and test-unseen (4,173 pairs); the main comparison reports val-unseen and Table 2 reports test-unseen. Uses the known navigation-graph setting; success means stopping within 3 m of the goal. Reports TL, NE, SR, and SPL. Training data is augmented with 1M speaker-generated instructions.

datasets.name: Room-Across-Room (RxR)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the English subset (en-IN and en-US), using the val-unseen split (4,551 path-instruction pairs); reports NE, SR, SDTW, and NDTW in the known navigation-graph setting, with success defined as stopping within 3 m of the goal. For the object-reference analysis, randomly samples 500 val-unseen instructions, extracts nouns with an NLP parser, manually removes direction, scene, and other non-object references, then divides instructions into 6-or-more versus fewer-than-6 object references (354 and 146 instructions, respectively).

baselines.name: VLN ↻ BERT (OSCAR initialization; reproduced implementation)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the released VLN ↻ BERT implementation; the paper states that its baseline and SOAT use the same hyperparameters. Both use OSCAR initialization for the direct comparison.

baselines.name: VLN ↻ BERT (OSCAR initialization; original reported results)

metrics.name: Navigation Error (NE)
metrics.caveat: Does not explicitly measure path adherence; on RxR the paper also reports NDTW and SDTW, which explicitly measure path adherence.

metrics.name: Success Rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: Does not explicitly measure path adherence; on RxR the paper also reports NDTW and SDTW, which explicitly measure path adherence.

metrics.name: Success weighted by normalized inverse of Path Length (SPL)
Success weighted by normalized Dynamic Time Warping (SDTW)

controls.name: VLN ↻ BERT reference model
controls.detail: The unmodified VLN ↻ BERT baseline is evaluated alongside SOAT.
controls.rules_out: A difference against this reference measures the effect of the proposed approach relative to the existing navigation model.

controls.name: Object features added without the proposed architectural changes
controls.detail: Adds object features to VLN ↻ BERT, with no selective attention or view aggregation.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether simply adding object features explains the gains; this condition slightly reduces val-unseen performance relative to the baseline.

controls.name: Object features with view aggregation only
controls.detail: Uses object features and view aggregation, but not selective attention.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether view aggregation alone accounts for the gains.

controls.name: Object features with selective attention only
controls.detail: Uses object features and selective attention, but not view aggregation.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether selective attention alone accounts for the gains.

controls.name: Selective attention without object features
controls.detail: Applies selective attention while omitting object features.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether selective attention without object features explains the full model’s result.

controls.name: No vision-and-language pretraining
controls.detail: Compares VLN ↻ BERT and SOAT without vision-and-language pretraining on R2R val-unseen.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether SOAT’s advantage appears without vision-and-language pretraining; the paper reports similar performance and interprets this as evidence that pretraining is crucial.

confounds.name: The improvement comes from merely adding object features, not from the proposed architectural changes
confounds.detail: If the gain were due simply to supplying extra object inputs, the object-feature-only version of VLN ↻ BERT should improve over the baseline.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The R2R ablation shows that adding object features without selective attention or view aggregation slightly reduces performance; the paper also evaluates the architectural changes separately and together.

confounds.name: The result is caused by one architectural change alone rather than the combined scene- and object-aware design
confounds.detail: View aggregation or selective attention alone could account for the reported improvement without the full proposed combination.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The R2R ablations evaluate view aggregation and selective attention separately, as well as selective attention without object features; the paper reports the largest gains when all three modifications are used together.

confounds.name: The gains reflect general navigation improvement rather than better use of object references
confounds.detail: A similar gain on instructions with few object references would not specifically support the claim that SOAT uses object cues more effectively.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On a randomly sampled set of 500 RxR val-unseen instructions, the paper compares subsets with at least 6 versus fewer than 6 manually filtered object references; the reported gains are larger on the object-heavy subset.

datasets.name: Room-to-Room (R2R)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on validation-seen, validation-unseen, and test sets; validation-seen shares environments with training, while validation-unseen (11 environments) and test (18 environments) use distinct environments. Reports NE, OSR, SR (success if the final position is within 3 m of the goal), and SPL. Results use single-turn evaluation with greedy action decoding. No evaluation episode count is specified.

baselines.name: Seq2Seq
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared without augmentation and with randomly sampled or APS-sampled augmented paths. Random sampling and APS each use 17K paths; navigation models train on augmented data for 50K iterations and are fine-tuned on original human-written instructions for 20K iterations. Baseline models use batch size 100, 512-unit LSTMs, learning rate 1e-4, and dropout 0.5.

baselines.name: Speaker-Follower
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared without augmentation and with randomly sampled or APS-sampled augmented paths. Random sampling and APS each use 17K paths; navigation models train on augmented data for 50K iterations and are fine-tuned on original human-written instructions for 20K iterations. Baseline models use batch size 100, 512-unit LSTMs, learning rate 1e-4, and dropout 0.5.

baselines.name: RCM
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared without augmentation and with randomly sampled or APS-sampled augmented paths. Random sampling and APS each use 17K paths; navigation models train on augmented data for 50K iterations and are fine-tuned on original human-written instructions for 20K iterations. Baseline models use batch size 100, 512-unit LSTMs, RL learning rate 1e-5, and dropout 0.5.

metrics.name: Success Rate weighted by Path Length (SPL)

controls.name: Randomly sampled augmented paths
controls.detail: The random-path condition uses 17K paths, matching the number adversarially sampled by APS; the paper also compares performance across different ratios of augmented paths used.
controls.rules_out: That improvements are due merely to adding augmented paths, rather than to APS selecting them adversarially.

controls.name: No augmented data
controls.detail: Each navigation baseline is also evaluated after training without augmented data.
controls.rules_out: That any observed improvement over the unaugmented model is simply the baseline’s performance without the augmentation intervention.

confounds.name: APS paths are merely harder, rather than useful training examples
confounds.detail: A higher training challenge alone would not establish that APS paths improve navigation; the same headline could reflect difficult paths without useful coverage.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare model performance on APS-sampled and randomly sampled augmented sets; the paper reports that the APS-trained Seq2Seq performs better on the randomly sampled set than the randomly trained model.

confounds.name: Gains come from augmentation in general, not adversarial path selection
confounds.detail: The improvement could result from adding training paths regardless of how they were sampled.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare APS-sampled augmentation against randomly sampled augmentation using the same 17K path count, and examine success rate across different augmentation ratios.

confounds.name: Too many pre-exploration steps produce overly complicated paths that hurt navigation
confounds.detail: The paper notes that additional exploration can expose the model to paths that are too complicated and may reduce performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure success rate at different numbers of pre-exploration steps; the reported results show a trade-off and identify best-performing step counts for Seq2Seq and Speaker-Follower.

evidence_standards.name: Single-turn greedy action decoding
evidence_standards.detail: The reported R2R results are run in a single turn and use greedy action decoding. No seeds, variance estimates, statistical tests, or decision margin for treating differences as real are specified.

datasets.name: RELLIS-3D
datasets.eval_protocol: Five-fold evaluation over its five sequences: train the segmentation network on four sequences and evaluate on the remaining sequence. Remap semantic classes to seven categories, project 2D ground-truth labels onto a 3D point cloud, and query the semantic map at each 3D ground-truth point; evaluate only queries for which the map identifies an occupied cell. Episode or trial count is not stated.

datasets.name: OffRoad
datasets.eval_protocol: Train and evaluate on distinct trajectory sequences, with RGB images manually annotated by experts. Remap semantic classes to seven categories, project 2D ground-truth labels onto a 3D point cloud, and query the semantic map at each 3D ground-truth point; evaluate only queries for which the map identifies an occupied cell. The paper also evaluates zero-shot mapping on OffRoad using segmentation networks trained on OffRoad, OffRoad-P, RUGD, or RELLIS-3D, without adaptation. Episode or trial count is not stated.

baselines.name: ConvBKI
baselines.fair_comparison: The learned kernel is derived from a pre-trained weight trained with RELLIS-3D; other fairness controls are not stated.

metrics.name: Intersection over Union (IoU)
metrics.caveat: Mapping evaluation excludes queries where the map identifies a cell as unoccupied, which can favor discontinuous maps; the paper also reports voxel semantic accuracy and, in ablations, voxel occupancy accuracy.

metrics.name: Mean IoU (mIoU)
metrics.caveat: Classes absent from an evaluation dataset are excluded from the average; the paper also reports voxel semantic accuracy and, in ablations, voxel occupancy accuracy.

controls.name: Continuous Categorical ablation (Prob. only)
controls.detail: Use the Continuous Categorical extension while leaving adaptive kernel length and uncertainty thresholding disabled; the table also includes a condition with all three components disabled.
controls.rules_out: A gain in this ablation over the all-disabled condition can be attributed to using continuous semantic probabilities rather than requiring the adaptive kernel or threshold.

controls.name: Adaptive kernel length ablation
controls.detail: Compare the Prob.+Adap. condition with Prob. only, with uncertainty thresholding disabled.
controls.rules_out: A difference isolates the contribution of adaptive kernel length when using continuous probabilities.

controls.name: Uncertainty threshold ablation
controls.detail: Compare the Prob.+Thr. condition with Prob. only, with adaptive kernel length disabled.
controls.rules_out: A difference isolates the contribution of uncertainty thresholding when using continuous probabilities.

controls.name: All proposed components disabled
controls.detail: The ablation condition with Prob., Adap., and Thr. all disabled.
controls.rules_out: Provides the reference for assessing the added components; the paper’s ablation table reports this condition as the no-component configuration.

confounds.name: The apparent semantic advantage could result from evaluating only occupied cells, favoring discontinuous maps
confounds.detail: The paper notes that S-CSM performs better on RELLIS-3D primarily because evaluation is restricted to occupied voxels from discontinuous maps.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper additionally reports voxel occupancy accuracy in the ablation study to measure geometric completeness; it does not include this measure in the main RELLIS-3D comparison table.

confounds.name: Improvement could be due to handling label inconsistency rather than the paper’s uncertainty estimation and adaptive kernel
confounds.detail: SEE-CSOM incorporates label inconsistency during mapping, which the paper says can improve off-road results by limiting propagation of inconsistent predictions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against SEE-CSOM on the reported mapping metrics; the paper reports better results for its method on the main OffRoad comparison and attributes this to EDL and the uncertainty-aware adaptive kernel.

confounds.name: Thresholding could improve semantic scores merely by discarding predictions and reducing map coverage
confounds.detail: The paper reports that uncertainty thresholding improves mapping performance but decreases geometric completeness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure voxel occupancy accuracy alongside semantic metrics in the ablations; the paper reports that combining adaptive kernel length with thresholding improves semantic performance while maintaining geometric completeness.

datasets.name: RELLIS-3D
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 3D semantic mapping; classes absent from the evaluation dataset are excluded when calculating mIoU. No split or episode count is specified.

datasets.name: OffRoad
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 3D semantic mapping; classes absent from the evaluation dataset are excluded when calculating mIoU. No split or episode count is specified.

controls.name: Adaptive kernel disabled; uncertainty thresholding disabled
controls.detail: Ablation condition with neither component enabled.
controls.rules_out: Whether the adaptive kernel or uncertainty thresholding contributes to the reported performance when compared with the full configuration.

controls.name: Adaptive kernel disabled; uncertainty thresholding enabled
controls.detail: Ablation condition that enables thresholding but not the adaptive kernel.
controls.rules_out: Whether uncertainty thresholding contributes without the adaptive kernel.

controls.name: Adaptive kernel enabled; uncertainty thresholding disabled
controls.detail: Ablation condition that enables the adaptive kernel but not thresholding.
controls.rules_out: Whether the adaptive kernel contributes without uncertainty thresholding.
